newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Australian budget looms large in busy week.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Australian budget looms large in busy week.

text.p: The Australian government's 1997/98 budget on Tuesday is likely to overshadow most other events in a busy week ahead, although the stock market is likely to be more focused on bank profits due later in the week.
ECONOMICS
The budget looms large over the week, even though most in the markets expect to be completely underwhelmed by it all.

The 1997/98 Budget is being categorised as a "steady-as-she-goes" one, where Treasurer Peter Costello carries on the fiscal tightening begun last year, but at a far less agressive pace than in 1996/97.
From a starting point deficit of around A$3.9 billion, the market expects around A$2 billion to be cut in the coming fiscal year, with the potential to be surprised by a smaller deficit.
"The way the budget is shaping up, it is more likely there will be positive rather than negative surprises on bottom line budget figures," ANZ Securities chief economist Phil Graham said.
As well, growth forecasts are expected to be stronger, reflecting the official outlook of an improving economy.
Certainly the lack of budget leaks and the public statements of Costello indicate there are likely to be few surprises.
Economists said that while last year's cuts were made to many areas of government spending, this time round the government could trim A$2 billion or so without affecting activity.
For example, by cancelling the planned government super contribution promised by the previous Labor government, there will be no impact on activity.
Also, asset sales, while not included in the underlying deficit, will produce interest savings that improve the bottom line.
Following the budget, the government will start selling it. Treasurer Peter Costello is due at the National Press Club for lunch on Wednesday and in Sydney that night.
And once the budget is released, the debate will focus on whether the government will be able to pass its measures through the Senate.
Apart from the budget, housing finance data on Monday is probably the most important in a bunch of secondary data this week.
And finally, RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane will deliver a speech in Melbourne in Thursday, with a topic associated with monetary policy and the economy.
Given the rather extensive testimony he gave before a parliamentary committee last week, it is unlikely anything new will come from the speech, apart from some possible comment on the budget.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Friday: 10-year bond yield 7.66 pct)
Bonds are expected to go into next Tuesday's 1997/98 federal budget in rallying mode on the expectation of very little or zero fixed-income supply in the forthcoming fiscal year.
There is also a hope, although it might not follow immediately, that another stout budget by Treasurer Costello could prompt a credit rating upgrade from the major U.S. agencies, analysts said.

Other than the budget and housing finance data on Monday, there is very little for the market to look at locally, which could leave the market vulnerable to movements in the U.S., which faces key inflation data.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri: US$0.7782/87, New York US$0.7779/84)
The fortunes of the Australian dollar this week are more likely to follow those of the U.S. dollar and the yen, than depend on expected positive fundamentals.
Interest rates are on hold, but base metal prices are rising and the budget is expected to be positive, so the Aussie should be well supported although it may not have the strength to rise.
"While there are positives, the market lacks good reasons to buy the Australian dollar, particularly when the U.S. dollar/yen is sliding," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economists said.

But with the U.S. dollar weakening significantly last week against the yen amid concerns the Japanese were seeking a stronger yen, the dollar may not be able to remain immune from the liquidation of Japanese offshore holdings.
Comments from Japan, and the U.S. dollar's losses have raised the prospect that the U.S. dollar's almost two year long rally was at an end.
However, traders said the market was confused over what authorities around the world were seeking in terms of exchange rates.
"Given the counterbalancing positives and negatives, we expect the Australian dollar will remain in a US$0.7750/7820 range for much of the coming week," the DMG team said.
Hanging over forex markets this week will be next week's FOMC meeting, with speculation in U.S. rates also adding to the confusion over the direction of the U.S. dollar.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ords Index 2,526.0)
The Australian sharemarket is looking for a market-friendly budget next week and generous results from two of the major banks that report after Tuesday's budget.
The local market scaled new heights last week to end the week on a record high.

Previous attempts at staying above the key psycological level of 2,500 have been short lived, but this level could become familar territory as the market was boosted by higher metal prices and a renewed rally in the bond market.
The Australian bourse has also showed a small degree of independence from Wall Street as it has steadily gained last week despite the wild swing in the Dow Industrials.
"I think on a five day outlook it is pretty positive," said David Preece, equities strategist at Bankers Trust Investment Bank.
"The few wild cards next week are a big correction in the U.S. or something in the budget that has not been anticipated. I would rate the chance of both of those occuring as pretty low," Preece said.
However there may be some nervousness in the U.S. market ahead of the Federal Open Markets Committee (FOMC) meeting on May 20, Preece said.
Building materials, aluminium and sugar group CSR Ltd kicks off the short earnings season when it reports its 1996/97 year results on Monday, a lower profit is expected.
On Tuesday, St George Bank Ltd is the first amongst the banks to report their half year results, followed by Westpac Banking Corp on Wednesday and National Australia Bank Ltd on Thursday.
Elsewhere, oil groups Santos and Novus Petroleum Ltd are due to hold their annual meetings next week.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
